what_its_for: Lofexidine is used to help reduce withdrawal symptoms when you stop taking opioids (such as heroin, oxycodone, or other narcotic pain medicines). It does not treat addiction itself, but it can make the withdrawal process more manageable by easing symptoms like sweating, muscle aches, stomach cramps, feeling anxious, and having a runny nose.
how_to_take: Take lofexidine by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablets whole. Try to take your doses evenly spaced throughout the day. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, because stopping too quickly can cause your blood pressure to rise rapidly. Your doctor will slowly lower your dose before you stop completely.
dosing: The usual dose is 3 tablets (0.54 mg each, for a total of 0.18 mg per tablet) taken 4 times a day during your withdrawal period, typically for up to 14 days. Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how you feel and your blood pressure readings. Do not take more than 4 tablets at one time or more than 16 tablets in one day unless your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose at the regularly scheduled time. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store lofexidine at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store it in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking lofexidine, as it can increase dizziness and lower your blood pressure even more. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing activities that require alertness until you know how this medicine affects you, because it can make you feel dizzy or drowsy. Be careful when standing up quickly from a sitting or lying position to avoid feeling faint. Avoid taking other medicines that lower blood pressure or cause drowsiness without first checking with your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a very slow or irregular heartbeat, feel faint or lose consciousness, have a sudden drop in blood pressure, feel extremely dizzy or lightheaded, have chest pain, or if your heart is pounding or racing. Also call your doctor if you feel more anxious, restless, or confused, or if your withdrawal symptoms are getting worse instead of better.
when_it_works: Lofexidine starts working within a few hours of your first dose to help ease withdrawal symptoms. Most people notice the biggest benefit during the first few days of treatment. The full course of treatment is usually about 5 to 7 days, but your doctor may prescribe it for up to 14 days depending on how you feel.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older) may be more sensitive to the blood pressure-lowering effects and dizziness caused by lofexidine — extra care is needed to avoid falls. People with heart problems, kidney disease, or liver disease should tell their doctor before taking this medicine, as the dose may need to be adjusted. It is not known if lofexidine is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This medicine is not approved for use in children under 17 years of age.
